title: Personal Pronoun Paradigm (First, Second Familiar, and Third Person)
description: Pettigrew (1912) and Grierson (1904) document the primary personal pronouns of Meiteilon: 1st person singular 'ei' (historically alternating with 'ai'), 2nd person singular familiar 'nang', and 3rd person singular honorific 'mahak'. Case inflections attach as postpositions (e.g. agentive -na, possessive -gi).
morphological_rule: PronounStem + CaseSuffix (e.g. ei + -na -> eina; nang + -gi -> nang-gi)

examples.translation_provenance: Direct English translation printed in Pettigrew 1912, p. 14.

reviewer_attribution.notes: Verified against Pettigrew 1912 Manipuri Grammar, p. 14 paradigm table.

notes: Pronoun stems are cognate across Tibeto-Burman: Proto-Tibeto-Burman *ŋa-y (1st person), *na-ŋ (2nd person).

title: Second-Person Register Contrast: Familiar (nang) vs. Honorific (nahak)
description: Meitei distinguishes social distance and deference in second-person address. The familiar form 'nang' is employed among intimates, peers, or toward younger individuals, while the honorific form 'nahak' (or plural 'nakhoi') is used to express formal respect.
morphological_rule: nang (familiar) vs. na-hak (stem na + honorific formative -hak)

reviewer_attribution.notes: Attested in Pettigrew 1912 and reaffirmed in Chelliah 1997, p. 102.

notes: Social deixis remains active in contemporary Manipuri spoken register.

title: Cardinal Numeral Prefixation (Vocalic a- and Nasal ma- Formatives)
description: Basic cardinal numerals in Meitei are formed by affixing prefixes to Proto-Tibeto-Burman numeral roots. Digits 1 to 3 take the vocalic prefix 'a-' (a-ma 1, a-ni 2, a-hum 3), whereas digits 4 and 5 attach the historic nasal prefix 'ma-' (ma-ri 4, ma-nga 5). When functioning as post-nominal quantifiers, the numeral follows the quantified noun phrase.

examples.source_ref: Grierson 1904 LSI Vol. III Part III, p. 54

reviewer_attribution.notes: Verified against Grierson 1904 LSI numeral table.

title: Indicative Verbal Negation via Suffixation (-te / -de)
description: Indicative negation in Meitei is expressed morphologically by appending the negative suffix '-te' directly to the verbal root. Following vowels or voiced sonorants, intervocalic lenition/voicing regularly surfaces the suffix as '-de'. The negative suffix displaces affirmative assertive endings.

examples.source_ref: Chelliah 1997 A Grammar of Meithei, p. 261 ex. (14b)
examples.translation_provenance: Shobhana L. Chelliah 1997 grammatical gloss and translation.

reviewer_attribution.notes: Verified in Chelliah 1997, p. 261; also attested in Pettigrew 1912, p. 39.

notes: Imperative negation contrasts by prefixing 'tou-' or suffixing prohibitive '-kanu'.

title: Progressive / Continuous Aspect Suffixation (-li / -ri)
description: The progressive aspect in Meitei signifies an action or process ongoing at reference time. It is realized by the suffix '-li', which alternates with '-ri' when immediately following an open syllable (vowel-final stem) via regular rhotacism.

examples.translation_provenance: Chelliah 1997, p. 203 morpheme analysis and translation.

reviewer_attribution.notes: Verified in Chelliah 1997, p. 203 and Pettigrew 1912, p. 35.

notes: Rhotacism /l/ -> [r] after vowels is a pervasive morphophonemic process in Meitei.

title: Canonical Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) Syntax & Agentive Marking
description: Meitei adheres to a strict canonical Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) head-final constituent order. Nominal arguments precede the verb phrase, modifiers precede head nouns, and postpositions follow their noun phrase heads. Transitive subjects typically receive the agentive/nominative suffix '-na'.
citation_locator: Page 22, Specimens of Meithei, Sentence No. 1

examples.english: A certain man had two sons.
examples.morpheme_gloss: mi ama-na macha-nupa ani lei (man one-AGT son-male two have)
examples.source_ref: Grierson 1904 LSI Vol. III Part III, p. 22
examples.translation_provenance: Grierson 1904, p. 22 official linguistic survey translation.

reviewer_attribution.notes: Verified against Grierson 1904 LSI Vol. III Part III opening text specimen.

notes: While SOV is canonical, discourse-motivated scrambling is permitted when pragmatic focus or topicalization is active.
